---

[[Perceptron|Perceptrons]] stacked: an [[Input Layer]], one or more [[Hidden Layer|hidden layers]],
an [[Output Layer]], every unit in a layer connected to every unit in the next. "MLP" and
"feedforward network" and "fully connected network" all mean this, and when someone says
[[Neural Network]] with no further qualification this is usually the thing.

Two properties define it, and both are worth stating because architectures like [[CNN]] break the
second:

- **Feedforward**: information moves one way, input to output. No cycles, so a [[Forward Pass]] is
  just a sequence of [[Matrix Multiplication|matrix multiplications]] with an
  [[Activation Function]] between each pair.
- **Fully connected**: every unit sees every unit of the previous layer. It assumes no structure in
  the input at all, which is exactly its weakness on images.

$$
\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)} = \sigma\!\left(W^{(\ell)} \mathbf{a}^{(\ell-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}\right)
$$

## What it fixed and what it cost

It computes XOR, which a single [[Perceptron]] cannot, and with a non-linear activation it can
approximate any continuous function given enough width. But the two ingredients that make it
trainable were not available in 1969: a differentiable activation ([[Sigmoid]], now [[ReLU]]) and
[[Back Propagation]] to turn the [[Loss Function]]'s gradient into an update for every
[[Weights|weight]], including the buried ones. See [[Perceptron]] for that history.

The cost is parameter count. Fully connected means layer sizes multiply: [[MNIST]]'s 784 inputs
into a single hidden layer of 100 units is already 78,400 weights plus 100
[[Bias Term|biases]], for one layer, on tiny images. Worse, flattening the image throws away the
fact that neighbouring pixels are related, so the network has to relearn that from data. **That is
the problem [[CNN]] exists to solve**, by weight sharing and local connectivity.
